title: The Mill at Lublin to the Cell at Kuibyshev: Erlich, the Bund, and the Country That Was Here
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Lublin, the Mill and the Heder

stops.name: Lublin, birth in the miller's house
stops.date_confidence: attested with a live conflict: the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur gives 13 April 1882, Polish Wikipedia gives only 'May 1882', English Wikipedia gives the year alone. The two reference works disagree on the month and the disagreement is left standing here. The 1881 variant reported in some summaries was not found in any source reached.
stops.campa: In Lublin, a town of the Russian Empire's Congress Poland, a son is born to Moyshe Erlich, who owns a mill. The father was a fervent Gerer Hasid in his youth and has since freed himself of it, joined the Hovevei Zion, entered Bene Moshe, the inner order of Ahad Ha'am's followers, and become one of that teacher's own men. The boy is named Hersh-Wolf. He will keep the Yiddish name over the Yiddish press and sign the Polish one, Henryk, on everything the Polish state ever asks of him. The mill stands somewhere in the town. No source names the street.
suggested_refs: The Erlich family mill at Lublin, unlocated in any reachable source
Bene Moshe, the inner order of Ahad Ha'am's Hovevei Zion, to which Moyshe Erlich belonged
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur entry on Henryk Erlich

stops.name: Lublin, the heder and the second tutor
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Bundist biographical accounts give the double education at about six years old, no institution is named, and the coordinates are a city-centre stand-in. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: At six he is put into heder, and at the same hour of his childhood a separate tutor comes to the house for the secular subjects. Two educations run alongside each other in one boy: the Hebrew of the sacred text in one room, arithmetic and Russian and Polish in the next. Thirty years on, the party he leads will refuse the same choice, a Jewish people wholly Jewish and wholly at home in the country it lives in. No source names the heder or the tutor. The building, if it stood, is not identified.
suggested_refs: The heders of Jewish Lublin before 1900, none identified with the Erlich household
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Warsaw, the law faculty and the gold medal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the faculty and the gold medal via the Leksikon; the year is given without a month, defaulted to January. The full sequence of his universities is reconstruction, not a checked academic record.
stops.campa: He finishes his gymnasium with a gold medal and enters the law faculty of the Imperial University of Warsaw, an institution teaching in Russian, in a Polish city, to a student who thinks in Yiddish. Warsaw in 1902 holds the largest Jewish population of any city in Europe and the densest network of clandestine circles in the empire, and the two overlap. Within the year he is inside both, the lecture hall in the morning and the illegal reading circle in the evening.
suggested_refs: The Krakowskie Przedmiescie campus of the Imperial University of Warsaw, still in use
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

segments.name: The Theatre, the Funeral, and the Wandering Studies

stops.name: Warsaw, the municipal theatre and Zloty Cielak
stops.date_confidence: the event is attested in the Leksikon: a 1902 demonstration during a performance of Zloty Cielak at the Warsaw municipal theatre, arrest, three weeks in jail. The building is inference only. No source names Teatr Wielki; 'municipal theatre' in 1902 Warsaw could equally mean Rozmaitosci or Teatr Letni. Month and day are arbitrary within the year.
stops.campa: The municipal theatre stages Zloty Cielak, The Golden Calf, an antisemitic play, and Jewish students break the performance up from inside the house. Erlich is among them. He is arrested and jailed three weeks, the first of a run of short sentences that will go on, under one government and then another, for the next twenty years. Somewhere in this same stretch of months he joins the General Jewish Labour Bund, the party that will hold him for the next thirty-seven years. He is twenty.
suggested_refs: Zloty Cielak, the antisemitic play whose 1902 Warsaw performance the students broke up
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur
Bundist biographical tradition (the 1903 date for joining the Bund is dossier tradition, not a checked party record)

stops.name: Warsaw, the funeral of Jozef Birencwajg
stops.date_confidence: attested: Polish Wikipedia dates the arrest to 4 May 1904, at the funeral of the socialist Jozef Birencwajg, during an attempt to lay a bouquet of red flowers on the coffin; the Leksikon confirms three months in jail and expulsion from the university and gives the name in Yiddish as Birntsvayg. The prison is inference: no source ties this detention to Pawiak, and the coordinates are a placeholder. The 'winter 1904' dating carried in some summaries is wrong.
stops.campa: The socialist Jozef Birencwajg is buried in Warsaw and the mourners turn the funeral into a demonstration. Erlich carries a bouquet of red flowers toward the coffin, and the flowers are the detail every account keeps. He is arrested for trying to lay them. Three months in prison follow, and then expulsion from the university, which ends his Russian legal education in Warsaw for good. The Bundist memorial literature keeps the dead man's name in its Yiddish form, Birntsvayg.
suggested_refs: Pawiak prison on ulica Dzielna, the standard Warsaw political prison of the period, not confirmed as the site of this detention
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Berlin, political economy under Unter den Linden
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from Bundist biographical accounts; not found in any of the sources fetched. The 1904-1905 window is traditional and the month is a placeholder for the academic year.
stops.campa: Expelled from Warsaw, he goes to the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universitat on Unter den Linden and reads political economy and political science. He is twenty-two, in his second country, studying the theory of a movement he has already been imprisoned for twice. The record does not say who paid for the term. Germany in these years is where the Second International keeps its brain: Kautsky, Bernstein, the revisionist quarrel, the machinery of a mass workers' party that actually functions.
suggested_refs: The Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universitat, Unter den Linden, Berlin

stops.name: Warsaw, Nasze Haslo
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the co-editorship with Bronislaw Grosser of the illegal Polish-language Bund organ is traditional, no editorial address survives, and the coordinates are a central-Warsaw placeholder. Month arbitrary within the 1905-1906 window.
stops.campa: The revolution of 1905 pulls him back to Warsaw. With Bronislaw Grosser he edits Nasze Haslo, the Bund's illegal Polish-language organ, illegal from its first issue to its last, printed and distributed under the noses of a police force that is losing its grip month by month. The choice of Polish is itself the argument: a Jewish workers' party addressing the Polish working class in its own language, on the ground both live on. The paper runs into 1906.
suggested_refs: Nasze Haslo, the Bund's clandestine Polish-language organ of 1905-1906

stops.name: Saint Petersburg University, the law degree
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Berlin-then-Petersburg sequence and the graduation around 1908 are traditional and were not confirmed against any academic record this pass. Month is a placeholder for the start of the course.
stops.campa: He resumes law at the university on the Universitetskaya Embankment, in the imperial capital itself, and takes his degree around 1908. A man twice expelled and twice imprisoned by the Russian state finishes that state's law course and qualifies to appear in its courts. Sofia Dubnov, daughter of the historian Simon Dubnov, is in the same student city. The exact order of his universities is reconstructed rather than documented, and the traditional accounts do not agree on the years.
suggested_refs: Saint Petersburg University on the Universitetskaya Embankment

stops.name: Paris, expelled from the Kingdom
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the imprisonment for Social Democratic party membership, the administrative expulsion from the Kingdom of Poland, and the Paris residence are all Bundist tradition. No address, no month, no arrival date. Canonical Paris pin, inherited byte-identical from the atlas.
stops.campa: More than three months in prison for membership of a Social Democratic party, and then an administrative order removing him from the Kingdom of Poland altogether. No address survives; the Bundist accounts give the city and nothing finer, which is how most of this decade of his life is recorded. He goes to Paris and lives there among the Russian and Jewish emigration, in the same cafes and reading rooms that hold every faction of the coming revolution in embryo.
suggested_refs: The Russian and Jewish emigre milieu of Paris before 1914

stops.name: Munich, the flight from the Bund case
stops.date_confidence: attested for the flight itself: the Leksikon has him hide in Kiev Province and depart for Munich in 1911. Nothing reached says the case was discontinued or that this is why he then went to Saint Petersburg, so that clause is dropped. Month arbitrary within the year.
stops.campa: A prosecution is opened against him and Bronislaw Grosser for membership of the Bund. He hides in Kiev Province while it develops, and when Grosser is arrested he goes further west still, to Munich. It is his third country of refuge in six years, and he is twenty-nine, with a law degree he cannot practise on and a party membership that is a criminal offence in the country he keeps returning to. Munich in 1911 is a city full of exiles who all expect to go home. What ended the case, or whether it simply lapsed, no source reached says.
suggested_refs: The 1911 Russian prosecution of Erlich and Bronislaw Grosser for Bund membership
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, marriage to Sofia Dubnov
stops.date_confidence: attested: Polish Wikipedia dates the marriage to September 1911, the Leksikon independently gives 1911. Sons Aleksander (1912-1985) and Wiktor (1914-2007) both born in Petersburg per Polish Wikipedia; the day-precise 22 November 1914 for Wiktor circulates but is carried by neither Polish Wikipedia nor the Leksikon and is not used here. No ceremony site located; canonical Petrograd pin.
stops.campa: In September he marries Sofia Dubnov, whom he met in this city. Her father is Simon Dubnov, historian of the Jewish diaspora and theorist of autonomism, and the marriage puts Erlich permanently inside the argument he will still be conducting with the old man twenty-seven years later, in print. Two sons follow, Aleksander in 1912 and Wiktor in 1914, both born in Petersburg, both of whom will outlive their father by decades in America. He also begins writing for the Russian daily Den.
suggested_refs: Sofia Dubnov-Erlich's own memoir of her father and her husband
The Russian daily Den, to which Erlich contributed from 1912
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Moscow, arrested among the shop clerks
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the arrest at the All-Russian Conference of commercial employees and the roughly three months in prison are Bundist tradition, the hall is not identified, and the month is a placeholder inside the traditional 'summer 1913'. Canonical Moscow pin.
stops.campa: He attends the All-Russian Conference of commercial employees in Moscow and is arrested there, and serves three months in prison again. The hall where the conference met is not identified in any account reached. The theatre in 1902, the funeral in 1904, the case that sent him to Paris, and now this: a qualified lawyer with a wife and two small sons in the capital, and every one of these sentences has so far ended in his release. He is thirty-one.
suggested_refs: The All-Russian Conference of commercial employees, Moscow, summer 1913

stops.name: Tauride Palace, the executive of the Soviet
stops.date_confidence: attested: English Wikipedia has him on the executive committee of the Petrograd Soviet in 1917, the Leksikon dates it from March. Coordinates corrected onto the Tauride Palace itself. Dates in Russia this year run Old Style until February 1918; the file uses the forms the sources print without converting them.
stops.campa: The Tsar is gone in March and the Petrograd Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies is sitting in the Tauride Palace, in the rooms the Duma used. Erlich is elected to its executive committee. Fifteen years of illegal presses and three-month sentences end inside a single season, and a Bundist lawyer from Lublin is helping govern the capital of the empire that jailed him. He is here for the months when the palace still holds it. The Soviet will move to the Smolny Institute later in the year.
suggested_refs: The Tauride Palace, seat of the Petrograd Soviet through most of 1917
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Petrograd, the tenth conference of the Bund
stops.date_confidence: attested: English Wikipedia's 'General Jewish Labour Bund' article dates the tenth conference to 14-17 April 1917 in Petrograd, the first held openly inside Russia, and names the committee formed afterward as Goldman, Erlich, Medem and Jeremiah Weinstein, dating the new committee to May. The same source states Medem remained in Poland and could not attend. Old Style dating not resolved.
stops.campa: From the fourteenth to the seventeenth of April the Bund holds its tenth conference openly inside Russia, the first time in twenty years the party has not had to meet abroad or in a cellar. Erlich sits among the delegates of the Central Committee. The committee formed afterward carries his name alongside Goldman, Jeremiah Weinstein, and Vladimir Medem, who is behind the German lines in Poland and cannot reach the room in which he is elected to it.
suggested_refs: The Bund's tenth conference, Petrograd, 14-17 April 1917

stops.name: Stockholm, the conference that never sits
stops.date_confidence: attested for the mission and for England, France and Italy via English Wikipedia; Sweden and Norway, and Stockholm's role as the intended conference site, come from Bundist tradition and were not reconfirmed. Month is a placeholder inside the summer.
stops.campa: The Petrograd Soviet sends a delegation west to convene an international socialist conference at Stockholm and end the war by agreement between the workers' parties of the belligerent states. Erlich travels with it. The neutral Swedish capital is the only ground on which Germans and Frenchmen and Russians could sit at one table. The Entente governments refuse their own socialists passports, and the delegation spends the summer arguing with the governments of its own allies. The conference is never held.
suggested_refs: The abortive Stockholm socialist peace conference of 1917

stops.name: London, the Entente shuts the road
stops.date_confidence: attested that the delegation travelled to England and France; the specific London and Paris scenes, and the month, are reconstruction from the general history of the Stockholm mission.
stops.campa: In England the delegation meets the British labour movement and the British government, and the government is the harder audience. He is carrying the authority of a revolutionary capital, and outside that capital it buys him very little. The war goes on because the men who might have stopped it cannot be got into the same room. Erlich crosses to France on the same errand and meets the same wall. Passports for Stockholm are withheld. The seamen's union refuses to carry delegates.
suggested_refs: The British government's refusal of passports to socialist delegates bound for Stockholm, 1917

stops.name: Rome, the last stage of the mission
stops.date_confidence: attested that the delegation reached Italy; the return to Petrograd in early August is Bundist tradition. The day is arbitrary within July.
stops.campa: Italy is the last stage of a mission that has failed in every capital it entered. The delegation puts its case to the Italian socialists and turns for home. He has spent the one summer in which a negotiated peace was arguable arguing for it, in four countries. By the beginning of August Erlich is in Petrograd again with nothing to report except refusal, in a city where the Provisional Government's authority is visibly draining and Kornilov is a few weeks from marching on it.
suggested_refs: The Italian Socialist Party's reception of the Petrograd Soviet delegation, summer 1917

stops.name: Mariinsky Palace, the walkout
stops.date_confidence: attested via the Leksikon, which gives 15 August 1917 for his selection to the Pre-Parliament and October 1917 for the withdrawal with the Bundist faction and the Mensheviks. The venue is identified from the general history of the body, not from a source specific to Erlich; coordinates corrected onto the Mariinsky Palace. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: He is chosen in August to the Provisional Council of the Russian Republic, the Pre-Parliament, which sits in the Mariinsky Palace on St Isaac's Square. He is thirty-five, and has spent the most consequential year in Russian history on the losing side of it. In October, at its second session, he walks out with the Bundist faction and the Mensheviks. Within days the Bolsheviks take the Winter Palace and the question of who sat in the Pre-Parliament stops mattering to anybody.
suggested_refs: The Mariinsky Palace, seat of the Provisional Council of the Russian Republic, autumn 1917
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Petrograd, Rabochaia gazeta
stops.date_confidence: the editorial board membership is Bundist tradition, office address not located, coordinates approximate. The May 1918 Menshevik conference, where he represented the Bund's Northern bureau, is attested in English Wikipedia's 'General Jewish Labour Bund' and is folded into this stop rather than given a place of its own, since no source names the venue.
stops.campa: After October he joins the editorial board of Rabochaia gazeta, the Menshevik central paper, which puts his name on the masthead of the opposition. The following May he is at the Menshevik party conference representing the Bund's Northern bureau. The position he takes in these months he holds for the rest of his life: that a socialism which abolishes the workers' own liberty to organise, publish and vote is not socialism, whatever it calls itself. The Bolsheviks suppress the paper in 1918.
suggested_refs: Rabochaia gazeta, central organ of the Mensheviks, suppressed by the Bolsheviks in 1918

stops.name: Lublin, the road back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the family's return from Russia via Lublin in August 1918 is Bundist tradition and was not itemised in any of the encyclopedia entries checked. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: With Sofia and the boys he crosses out of revolutionary Russia and comes to Lublin, the town of the mill and the heder, thirty-six years after he was born in it. Poland is about to be a state again for the first time since 1795, and the Bund will be a legal party in it. The Jewish town he was born into is still there, and still growing. Whatever he thought, standing in his birthplace at the end of the Russian empire, no account records. They stay two months.
suggested_refs: Jewish Lublin on the eve of Polish independence

stops.name: Warsaw, the family settles
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the October date; the fact of resettlement in Warsaw is not in dispute. Canonical Warsaw pin, inherited byte-identical from the atlas. The quote is written twenty years later and is placed here as a statement of the position, not as speech at this moment.
stops.campa: In October the family moves to Warsaw and does not move again for twenty-one years. He is thirty-six. Erlich resumes party work in a country where the Bund can now stand in elections, print without a censor, and run its own schools, unions, sanatoria, youth movement, sports clubs and daily paper. The doctrine is doikayt, hereness: the Jewish future is made where Jews already live, in Yiddish, alongside the Polish workers' movement and not instead of it.
stops.quote: The Bund has therefore always and constantly thought of itself as an organic part of the Jewish people.
stops.quote_source: Henryk Erlich, 'Is Zionism a Liberating Democratic Movement? (A Reply to Professor Simon Dubnow)', Di Tsukunft, October 1938, trans. Samuel A. Portnoy; written twenty years after this stop
suggested_refs: Doikayt, the Bund's doctrine of hereness
sources: Henryk Erlich, 'Is Zionism a Liberating Democratic Movement?', Di Tsukunft, October 1938, trans. Samuel A. Portnoy (libcom.org)

stops.name: Plac Bankowy, head of the list
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Leksikon for March 1919, that he was named to head the Bund's candidate list for the Warsaw city council. The frequently repeated result, four Bundists seated, appears in no source reached and is not stated here. Canonical Plac Bankowy pin, inherited byte-identical from victor_alter.journey.json; the historic town hall itself sits about 130 metres west.
stops.campa: In March he is named to head the Bund's candidate list for the Warsaw city council, and the party enters the municipal government of the Polish capital. The council chamber at the old town hall on Plac Bankowy becomes his second desk beside the editorial one, and municipal Warsaw, its housing and its schools and its sanitation and its Jewish quarter of some three hundred thousand people, becomes his subject as much as the international question. How many Bundists took seats on that first list is not stated in any source reached.
suggested_refs: The Warsaw city council chamber at the old town hall, Plac Bankowy
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Plac Bankowy, three months for a speech
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Leksikon: 1920, Russo-Polish war, arrested, three months in jail for an anti-war speech at the city council. Venue, cause and sentence all confirmed. The further claim, of a separate Bund-membership prosecution dragging three years before dismissal, is in no source reached and is omitted. Month placed at the crisis of the war; day defaulted.
stops.campa: The Red Army is at the Vistula and Poland is fighting for its existence. Erlich stands in the city council chamber and speaks against the war. He opposes the Bolsheviks and he opposes the war against them. He is arrested for the speech and serves three months, his first imprisonment by the Polish Republic, a state not yet two years old, and the same sentence the Tsar's courts used to hand him. The chamber is the one he entered the year before at the head of the Bundist list.
suggested_refs: The Bund's anti-war position during the Polish-Soviet War of 1920
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Krakow, the unification conference
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 1920 Krakow unification conference and Erlich's entry to the Central Committee are Bundist tradition, the hall is not identified, coordinates are central Krakow, and the month is a placeholder within the year.
stops.campa: The Bund's separate wartime fragments meet at Krakow to become one party in one country. Erlich enters the Central Committee and comes out of the conference its leading political voice. For the next twenty-one years his name travels with one other through the Polish press, the International, the police files, and finally the NKVD's paperwork, where the two are entered as a single case. The other is Wiktor Alter, eight years younger, an engineer trained in Belgium, already deported to Siberia and escaped from it.
suggested_refs: The Bund's 1920 unification conference at Krakow

stops.name: Warsaw, the Folkstsaytung
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the co-editorship of the Folkstsaytung from 1921 and the eventual editorship-in-chief. The Glos Bundu confiscations, the two convictions as responsible editor and the amnesties are Bundist tradition. No street address located for either paper; coordinates place the stop in the historic Jewish press district. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He begins writing for the Yiddish daily Folkstsaytung, becomes its editor, and in time its editor-in-chief. The paper, later the Naye Folkstsaytung, is the nervous system of an entire counterculture: the unions, the schools teaching in Yiddish, the youth movement, the sanatoria, the cooperatives, the sports clubs. He also edits the Polish-language weekly Glos Bundu, whose issues the authorities confiscate and for which the courts twice sentence him as responsible editor, both judgments extinguished by amnesty. He is at that desk until September 1939.
suggested_refs: The Naye Folkstsaytung, Warsaw Yiddish daily of the Bund
Glos Bundu, the Bund's Polish-language weekly

stops.name: Grzybowska Street, five of fifty
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia: elected to the Warsaw kehilla council in 1924 as one of five Bundists among fifty members. The presidential run against Eliahu Kirszbraun that circulates for this year is in no source reached and is a conflation with the documented 1936 contest; it is omitted. The community building's address is inferred, not confirmed. Month and day defaulted. The quote is from 1938 and states the position, not words spoken here.
stops.campa: The Warsaw kehilla, the official Jewish community council, is the one arena in which Jewish parties govern Jews directly, and the Bund contests it as it contests everything else. Its position inside the kehilla is its position everywhere: the Jewish future is here, in Poland, in Yiddish, and the community's money should be spent on that assumption. Erlich is elected in 1924 as one of five Bundists in a body of fifty, a small and loud minority among Agudists, Zionists and assimilationists.
stops.quote: We stated that Zionism was not and could not be a solution to the Jewish question.
stops.quote_source: Henryk Erlich, 'Is Zionism a Liberating Democratic Movement? (A Reply to Professor Simon Dubnow)', Di Tsukunft, October 1938, trans. Samuel A. Portnoy; written fourteen years after this stop
suggested_refs: The Warsaw kehilla council and its elections between the wars
sources: Henryk Erlich, 'Is Zionism a Liberating Democratic Movement?', Di Tsukunft, October 1938, trans. Samuel A. Portnoy (libcom.org)

segments.name: The International, the Kehilla, and the Reply to Dubnov

stops.name: Hamburg, the Socialist International
stops.date_confidence: attested via the Leksikon, which has Erlich attending Socialist International congresses as a Bund delegate at Hamburg 1923, Marseille 1925 and Vienna 1931; Polish Wikipedia records his membership of the Socialist International Executive from 1930. The often-repeated claim that the Polish Bund was admitted to the Labour and Socialist International in 1930-1931 does not survive those earlier delegations and is not used. The congress hall is not identified; the day is the opening of the Hamburg unity congress.
stops.campa: He goes to Hamburg as the Bund's delegate to the congress of the Socialist International, the first of the great postwar reunification congresses and the first of a string he will attend: Marseille in 1925, Vienna in 1931, three congresses in eight years. A party of Yiddish-speaking Polish workers now holds a seat at the table where European social democracy decides what it thinks. In 1930 he is elected to the Executive of the Labour and Socialist International itself.
suggested_refs: The 1923 Hamburg congress at which the Labour and Socialist International was founded
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Vienna, the congress and the Executive
stops.date_confidence: attested via the Leksikon for the Vienna congress as a Bund delegate; the day is the opening of the LSI's Vienna congress and the hall is not identified. Central Vienna coordinates.
stops.campa: Vienna in 1931 is the showpiece of European social democracy: the municipal housing blocks, the workers' schools, the Karl-Marx-Hof, a whole city administered by a socialist party inside a state that is not socialist. In three years the Austrian workers' movement will be shelled out of those housing blocks by its own government's artillery. The congress of the Socialist International meets there and Erlich sits in it for the Bund, a member of the Executive since the year before.
suggested_refs: The 1931 Vienna congress of the Labour and Socialist International
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Warsaw, In kamf farn revolutsyonern sotsyalizm
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pamphlet is catalogued in the standard Bund bibliography and by the Yiddish Book Center digitisation programme, but the catalogue record was not opened this pass. Month and day defaulted; the stop sits at the Folkstsaytung pin, not at a located press.
stops.campa: He publishes a pamphlet, In kamf farn revolutsyonern sotsyalizm, In the Struggle for Revolutionary Socialism, and it names both enemies at once. Against the reformists, who have decided that socialism arrives by waiting. Against the Communists, who have built a dictatorship and call it the workers' state. It is addressed to Jewish workers in Warsaw and Lodz who are being told, from two directions at once, to give up on themselves. Hitler has been in office a year.
suggested_refs: In kamf farn revolutsyonern sotsyalizm (Warsaw, 1934), digitised by the Yiddish Book Center
sources: Bund bibliography as summarised in secondary literature; catalogue record not independently opened

stops.name: Grzybowska Street, sixteen votes
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the Bund's fifteen seats of fifty, Erlich's sixteen votes, and Jakub Trokenheim's winning nineteen. The figure of ten votes for Yitzhak Schipper, which circulates alongside these, is in no source reached and is omitted. The public accusation against Grunbaum and Jabotinsky is described consistently in secondary summaries but was not verified against a primary 1936 press account. Month and day are placeholders. The quote is the same charge in its 1938 printed form.
stops.campa: The kehilla election gives the Bund fifteen of fifty seats, and Erlich stands for the presidency of the Warsaw Jewish community. He takes sixteen votes. Jakub Trokenheim of Agudath Israel wins with nineteen. In the aftermath he turns on the Zionist leaders in public, Yitzhak Grunbaum and Zeev Jabotinsky by name, and charges them with doing the antisemites' work: telling Polish Jews they have no future in Poland is what the men demanding their emigration are saying, in the same years, to the same people. He is fifty-four.
stops.quote: Over the years, Zionism has evolved into an open ally of our deadly enemy—anti-Semitism.
stops.quote_source: Henryk Erlich, 'Is Zionism a Liberating Democratic Movement? (A Reply to Professor Simon Dubnow)', Di Tsukunft, October 1938, trans. Samuel A. Portnoy; the charge in its published form, two years after this stop
suggested_refs: The 1936 Warsaw kehilla election and its presidential ballot
sources: Henryk Erlich, 'Is Zionism a Liberating Democratic Movement?', Di Tsukunft, October 1938, trans. Samuel A. Portnoy (libcom.org)

stops.name: Warsaw, the reply to Professor Dubnov
stops.date_confidence: the text itself is attested and was fetched verbatim in translation; the October 1938 Di Tsukunft publication is asserted by multiple secondary Bund summaries and was not confirmed against the periodical. Di Tsukunft was published in New York, so the stop is placed where Erlich wrote rather than where the issue was printed. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: Simon Dubnov, seventy-eight years old, the historian of the diaspora, his own father-in-law, has come out for Zionism, and Erlich answers him in print. He is arguing with his wife's father about where the Jews of Europe should be in ten years' time. The essay holds that Zionism feeds on Jewish persecution, that it accepts the antisemite's premise that Jews do not belong where they live, and that a Jewish state could never serve as a spiritual centre for the Jews of the goles.
stops.quote: Zionism, in point of fact, has always been a Siamese twin of anti-Semitism and of every kind of national chauvinism.
stops.quote_source: Henryk Erlich, 'Is Zionism a Liberating Democratic Movement? (A Reply to Professor Simon Dubnow)', Di Tsukunft, October 1938, trans. Samuel A. Portnoy
suggested_refs: Simon Dubnov's late writings on Zionism, to which the essay is a reply
Samuel A. Portnoy's English translation of the essay
sources: Henryk Erlich, 'Is Zionism a Liberating Democratic Movement?', Di Tsukunft, October 1938, trans. Samuel A. Portnoy (libcom.org, fetched verbatim)

stops.name: Warsaw, leaving on the sixth of September
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Bund Central Committee's general advice to go east and Erlich's departure on 6 or 7 September, intending to reach Vilna, are Bundist tradition. Canonical Warsaw pin.
stops.campa: The Germans crossed the border on the first. On the sixth the Bund Central Committee advises its people to go east, and Erlich leaves Warsaw on a road already full of that instruction. He is fifty-seven years old. He has lived in this city for twenty-one years, edited its Yiddish daily, sat on its council and stood for the presidency of its kehilla, and he will not see it again. The plan is to reach Vilna, in the far north-east, where the leadership means to reconstitute itself.
suggested_refs: The Bund Central Committee's September 1939 instruction to move east

stops.name: Brest, the railway station
stops.date_confidence: attested and undisputed: English Wikipedia, Polish Wikipedia and the Leksikon all give 4 October 1939 for the NKVD arrest at Brest, and Polish Wikipedia specifies the railway station. No source reached carries the 6 October variant. Coordinates are central Brest; the station lies roughly a kilometre north-west. Alter's arrest at Kowel on 29 September 1939 is attested in English Wikipedia's 'Victor Alter'.
stops.campa: Two invasions have met in the middle of Poland and the eastern half is Soviet now. The Bund is the oldest and best organised anti-Bolshevik socialist party in Eastern Europe, and its leaders have been arguing against the Soviet state in print since 1918. Wiktor Alter had been taken at Kowel five days earlier, before the Germans and the Soviets had even finished dividing the country between them. At the railway station in Brest, on the fourth of October, the NKVD arrests him.
suggested_refs: Brest railway station, site of the arrest of 4 October 1939
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Moscow, the Lubyanka
stops.date_confidence: attested: Polish Wikipedia has him imprisoned in the Lubyanka in Moscow from October 1939. The transfer after roughly two weeks in Brest prison is tradition, and the day is a placeholder. The isolation, sleep deprivation and personal interrogation by Beria carried in Bundist accounts appear in none of the sources reached and are named in the campa as tradition only. Coordinates corrected onto the building.
stops.campa: After roughly two weeks in Brest prison he is moved to Moscow and into the Lubyanka. The investigation that follows will take two years and produce a case: that the Bund's leader is an agent of Polish intelligence, or of the Germans, or of both, the charge shifting with the season and the state of Soviet foreign policy. Bundist tradition adds isolation, sleep deprivation, and Beria interrogating him in person. None of that is in the documents reached here.
suggested_refs: The Lubyanka, NKVD headquarters and prison, Moscow

stops.name: Butyrka, the second Moscow prison
stops.date_confidence: the Butyrka detention is attested in English Wikipedia. The claim that the NKVD compelled him to write extensive histories of the Bund and its personnel is in no source reached and is omitted. Alter's Butyrka detention from 9 December 1939 through twenty months of interrogation is attested in his own file. Canonical Butyrka pin, inherited byte-identical from victor_alter.journey.json, though the prison building itself stands roughly 500 metres north-west of that point. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He is transferred to Butyrka, the other great Moscow prison, where Wiktor Alter is held from December 1939 through twenty months of interrogation. The pact with Germany holds. The Bund's press is gone, its schools are gone, Warsaw is under German occupation, and the Jews of the quarter Erlich represented on the city council are being walled into a district of it. Whether either man ever knew he was in the same building as the other, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Butyrka prison, Moscow

stops.name: Saratov, the second of August
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1941, and the commonly repeated 1940 is an error. Polish Wikipedia gives 2 sierpnia 1941 and the Leksikon gives 2 August 1941 with the commutation to ten years; the Leksikon also has the Saratov transfer in summer 1941, and Polish Wikipedia has him in the Lubyanka from October 1939, which makes English Wikipedia's 2 August 1940 internally impossible. Coordinates moved to central Saratov; no prison building identified.
stops.campa: By the summer of 1941 the Germans are inside the Soviet Union and the prisoners are being moved east. In Saratov, on the Volga, a tribunal sentences him to death on the second of August. The sentence is commuted to ten years in the camps, and six weeks after that he is a free man, because a Polish government-in-exile in London and a Soviet government at war have signed an agreement emptying Soviet prisons of Polish citizens. Between the sentence and the commutation he spends roughly two weeks in the condemned cell.
suggested_refs: The Saratov NKVD prison and tribunal, summer 1941
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur
Wikipedia, 'Henryk Erlich' (gives 1940, treated here as erroneous)

stops.name: Moscow, released under Sikorski-Mayski
stops.date_confidence: the enabling agreement is attested, signed in London on 30 July 1941 by Sikorski and Ivan Mayski. The day of Erlich's own release is contested: the Leksikon gives 11 September 1941 with Alter freed on the 12th, Polish Wikipedia gives 12 September for Erlich himself, and Alter's own file has him released on 13 September. Moscow is inference; no source names a release city. The reported acknowledgement by Beria of a fatal error is in none of the sources reached. Canonical Moscow pin.
stops.campa: The Sikorski-Mayski agreement, signed in London on the thirtieth of July by General Sikorski and Ambassador Ivan Mayski, restores relations between Poland and the USSR and amnesties Polish citizens in Soviet hands. Erlich walks out on the eleventh of September, Alter within a day or two of him. They are received at the Polish embassy. In the same weeks Soviet officials propose that the two of them organise a Jewish anti-fascist committee to raise support for the Soviet war effort in the West.
suggested_refs: The Sikorski-Mayski agreement, London, 30 July 1941
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Kuibyshev, the evacuated embassy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the autumn 1941 evacuation to Kuibyshev, and English Wikipedia places Erlich at the Polish embassy there. The Grand Hotel named in some accounts is confirmed by nothing reached and is dropped. Canonical Kuibyshev pin, inherited byte-identical from victor_alter.journey.json. Day taken from Alter's file, where the evacuation stop is dated 15 October 1941.
stops.campa: With the Germans closing on Moscow the government and the diplomatic corps are evacuated six hundred miles east to Kuibyshev on the Volga, and Erlich and Alter go with the Polish mission. Nine weeks earlier they were under sentence of death in the same state's prisons. They are housed in connection with the embassy, in privileged conditions, drafting the structure of the committee they have been asked to found and corresponding with Jewish labour organisations in New York and London.
suggested_refs: The evacuated Polish embassy at Kuibyshev, autumn 1941

stops.name: Kuibyshev, the fourth of December
stops.date_confidence: attested: English Wikipedia on both men and Polish Wikipedia give the night of 3-4 December 1941. The Leksikon dissents with October 1941, a minority reading. Two details often attached to this arrest are not carried by any source reached and are excluded: the secretly recorded conversations about the killing of Polish officers, and a Soviet citizenship decree said to have immediately preceded it. Canonical Kuibyshev pin.
stops.campa: On the night of the third to the fourth of December the NKVD takes them both again. No charge is announced, no trial follows, and the Polish embassy whose guests they were is told nothing that means anything. What changed between September and December has never been documented. Bundist accounts point to conversations recorded in their rooms, including talk of the missing Polish officers; the sources reached here do not carry it. They simply disappear.
suggested_refs: The Polish government-in-exile's protests over the December 1941 disappearance of Erlich and Alter
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur (dissenting: October 1941)

stops.name: Kuibyshev, the bars of the cell window
stops.date_confidence: the manner of death is attested and stated plainly: the Leksikon says he hanged himself in his Kuibyshev cell, Polish Wikipedia describes suicide by hanging from the bars of the cell window. The day is contested: English Wikipedia and the Leksikon give 15 May 1942, Polish Wikipedia gives 14 May 1942. No burial site is known and no autopsy or family identification is on record. Canonical Kuibyshev pin, inherited byte-identical; no prison building is located.
stops.campa: He hangs himself from the bars of his cell window in the NKVD prison at Kuibyshev, on the fourteenth or the fifteenth of May, 1942. There is no grave, no autopsy that anyone outside the ministry ever saw, no notification sent to his wife or to either of his two sons, and no body returned to anyone. Wiktor Alter is alive in another cell and will be shot the following February, and in between the Soviet state will tell the world that the two of them were executed together. He is sixty years old.
suggested_refs: The post-Soviet NKVD file on the Erlich case, source of the documented suicide
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, translation of the Leksikon fun der nayer yidisher literatur

stops.name: Washington, the ambassador's letter
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the date and the substance: Maxim Litvinov informed American labour leaders including William Green of the AFL that the two men had been executed. The Warsaw ghetto rumour of letters signed 'Henryk Wiktor' is reported as a wartime legend, not a documented fact, and is folded in here as such. The stop is placed at the Soviet embassy in Washington because that is where the announcement was made; Erlich had been dead nine months.
stops.campa: Maxim Litvinov, Soviet ambassador to the United States, tells William Green of the American Federation of Labor that Erlich and Alter have been executed for urging Soviet troops to make peace with Germany. Erlich has been dead nine months by his own hand. Alter has been shot within the last week. In the Warsaw ghetto that same February, letters signed Henryk Wiktor, the two first names fused into one man, are being passed hand to hand as proof that both of them are alive.
suggested_refs: The Litvinov statement of 23 February 1943 and the American labour movement's response

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the gedenk-bukh
stops.date_confidence: the Buenos Aires 1943 memorial volume, Henrik Erlikh un Viktor Alter, is a dossier-derived lead that was not independently refetched; Open Library independently holds the New York editions of 1943 and 1951 and the American Bund pamphlet The Case of Henryk Erlich and Victor Alter (New York, 1943). Canonical Buenos Aires pin, inherited byte-identical. Month and day arbitrary within the year.
stops.campa: The Bundist emigration begins publishing its dead. A memorial volume, Henrik Erlikh un Viktor Alter, appears in Buenos Aires, where Jewish Poland's labour movement has had a second home since the century turned; another comes out in New York, and the American Representation of the Bund issues a pamphlet, The Case of Henryk Erlich and Victor Alter, demanding an accounting from Moscow. The memorial literature fixes the death at December 1942 and repeats it for half a century.
suggested_refs: Henrik Erlikh un Viktor Alter, memorial volume, Buenos Aires 1943 (lead not independently verified)
The living record of two leaders of labor (Erlich-Alter Memorial Conference), catalogued at both 1942 and 1943
Samuel A. Portnoy's 1990 English edition, Henryk Erlich and Victor Alter
sources: Dossier lead for the Buenos Aires edition, not independently refetched

stops.name: Okopowa Street, the cenotaph
stops.date_confidence: attested by English and Polish Wikipedia for the date, 17 April 1988. The communist government's opposition, Marek Edelman's and Solidarity's role and the attendance above three thousand are reported in the same articles and are treated here as reported rather than documented. Coordinates inherited from the same monument's stop in victor_alter.journey.json; the two lenses of this dossier gave two different and both erroneous points for it.
stops.campa: A stone goes up in the Jewish cemetery on Okopowa Street for two men with no graves. Poland's communist government opposes the monument and it is obtained anyway, through Marek Edelman, who commanded in the ghetto uprising and stayed a Bundist to the end of his life, and through Solidarity. The inscription says the two were executed in the Soviet Union, which is the account the world was given in 1943 and not the account in the files. Over three thousand people come to the unveiling.
stops.quote: Leaders of the Bund, Henryk Erlich, b. 1882, and Wiktor Alter, b. 1890. Executed in the Soviet Union.
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the Erlich-Alter cenotaph, Jewish Cemetery, Okopowa Street, Warsaw, unveiled 17 April 1988, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Victor Alter'
suggested_refs: The Erlich-Alter cenotaph, Okopowa Street Jewish Cemetery, Warsaw

stops.name: Moscow, the eighth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia's 'Victor Alter' for the date and for the notification of Victor Erlich. The widely repeated attribution to 'Russian president Boris Yeltsin' is anachronistic twice over and is corrected here: the USSR did not dissolve until December 1991, and Yeltsin was Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the RSFSR from 29 May 1990 and became President of Russia only on 10 July 1991. Canonical Moscow pin.
stops.campa: The repressions against Erlich and Alter are declared unlawful and both men are formally rehabilitated, forty-nine years after the fact. Boris Yeltsin, who chairs the Supreme Soviet of the Russian republic and is not yet president of anything, signs. Wiktor Erlich, professor of Slavic literature at Yale, is officially informed that the state which killed his father was wrong to have done it. The Soviet Union still exists, and has ten months left to it.
suggested_refs: The 8 February 1991 rehabilitation decree in the Erlich-Alter case
